v: Calgary's Chinatown was forced to move. Twice.
Today it sits at the foot of the Centre Street Bridge. But it didn't start here.
The first Chinatown grew up just east of the train station, where the City's Municipal Building stands today.
In eighteen ninety-two, a smallpox outbreak fuelled violence. A mob of more than three hundred men smashed the doors and windows of Chinese laundries.
For three weeks, the North West Mounted Police had to protect Chinatown.
In nineteen-oh-one, anti-Chinese sentiment and development pressure prompted a second Chinatown, across the railway tracks on Tenth Avenue Southwest.
Then, in nineteen-ten, the Canadian Northern Railway announced its route into Calgary. Property values soared. Landlords evicted their Chinese tenants, and sold.
So a group of Chinese merchants bought land of their own, at Centre Street and Second Avenue.
Anti-Chinese protesters demanded Chinatown go somewhere else. The merchants won a permit, and built the Canton Block. It still stands.
In the nineteen-sixties, a proposed road would have wiped out half of Chinatown. The community organized, and the plan was defeated.
In nineteen ninety-two, the Chinese Cultural Centre opened, modelled on Beijing's Temple of Heaven.
Pushed out twice. Since nineteen-ten, Chinatown has stayed put.
